title: ⭐⭐ Practice: sorting nouns, ranking figures, naming who decides

questions.prompt: Complete this line from a report on a school campaign in Nabeul: "On Thursday the volunteers handed out a large number of ___ in front of the gate."
questions.explanation: "leaflets" is the only word that can follow a large number of: number of counts separate objects, and it counts them in the plural. "poster" names an object you can count too, but it is left in the singular, and number of never takes a singular noun; a large number of posters would have been correct. "information" and "advice" are both uncountable, so no number can reach them: English measures them with an amount of, a large amount of information, and never counts them one by one.

questions.prompt: The word "paper" belongs to both columns of the table, and its meaning changes with the column. In which of these four sentences is it used as a countable noun?

options.text: The stand ran out of paper before eleven o'clock.
We wrapped the leaflets in brown paper.
Rania bought a paper on her way to school.

questions.explanation: "Rania bought a paper on her way to school." uses paper countably: the article a is the proof, and the word no longer means the material at all but one object, a newspaper. "The stand ran out of paper before eleven o'clock." speaks of the material in a mass, with no article and no plural. "We wrapped the leaflets in brown paper." does the same: brown paper is a quantity you cut, not a number of objects. And "Paper is cheaper than cardboard." compares two materials in general, which is why the verb is singular and no article appears.

questions.prompt: The caretaker of a youth centre in El Kef explains his evening: "The director has me lock the two workshops at six." What does his sentence say about the director?

options.text: She forbids the caretaker to lock the workshops.
She asks somebody whose job it is to do it.
She locks the two workshops herself every evening.
She gives the caretaker permission to lock them.

questions.explanation: "She asks somebody whose job it is to do it." is what have somebody do something expresses: a request, or a weak obligation, arranged with the person whose work it already is. "She gives the caretaker permission to lock them." is the meaning of let, and permission is not what is at stake here: locking up is part of the job, not a favour the caretaker asked for. "She forbids the caretaker to lock the workshops." says the opposite of the sentence. And "She locks the two workshops herself every evening." misses the whole point of a causative verb: have somebody do something means precisely that somebody else does it.

questions.prompt: Three groups presented a poster on conflict at school. The jury gave 18 out of 20 to the first group, 11 to the second and 15 to the third. Complete the report: "The second group's poster was ___ of the three."
questions.explanation: "the worst" is the form: three posters are being ranked, so the sentence needs a superlative, and bad is one of the six irregular adjectives, bad, worse, the worst. "the baddest" adds the regular ending -est to an adjective that refuses it, the way a learner regularises an irregular verb. "the worse" puts the article of the superlative in front of the comparative form, so it belongs to neither. And "worse than" is the comparative, which compares two things and calls for a second element after than, whereas of the three announces a ranking.

questions.prompt: Read this notice printed on a school poster in Bizerte: "Our survey. 240 pupils answered our questions. 180 of them said they had seen a quarrel in the corridor this term. 60 of those 180 said they had tried to calm it down. No pupil was asked to give a name." Which statement do these figures allow you to make?

options.text: The survey gives the names of the pupils who quarrelled in the corridor.
Three quarters of the school saw a quarrel this term.
The sixty pupils who saw no quarrel did not answer.
Most of those who saw a quarrel did not try to calm it.

questions.explanation: "Most of those who saw a quarrel did not try to calm it." is the one the figures support: 180 saw a quarrel, 60 of them stepped in, so 120 did not, which is two out of three. "Three quarters of the school saw a quarrel this term." turns 180 out of 240 into a share of the whole school, but 240 is the number of pupils who answered, and the notice never says how many pupils the school has. "The sixty pupils who saw no quarrel did not answer." invents a fact: those 60 are inside the 240 who answered, and answering is exactly how we know about them. And "The survey gives the names of the pupils who quarrelled in the corridor." is contradicted by the last line of the notice.

questions.prompt: One word in this sentence has to be changed: "The association gave the pupils much useful advices about how to settle their conflicts." Which word is it?
questions.explanation: "advices" is the word to repair, into advice: the noun is uncountable and has one form only, whatever the number of pieces of advice given. "much" is already right, and right for that very reason, since much is the modifier an uncountable noun takes; a pupil who changes it into many is repairing the half of the phrase that was not broken. "conflicts" is correct as it stands: a conflict counts, one conflict, several conflicts, and it must not be dragged into the uncountable column just because violence and anger belong there. And "gave" is the ordinary past simple of give, with nothing wrong with it.
